Excellencies, distinguished colleagues, I hereby declare open the 17th meeting of the 63rd session of the Human Rights Council. Excellencies, distinguished participants, we will now continue the general debate under agenda item 3. We shall proceed with the list of observers of the Council. I give the floor to the distinguished representative of Eritrea via a video message.

Thank you, Mr. President. Item 3 lies at the core of this Council's mandate, the advancement of all human rights, including the right to development. Human rights are indivisible and mutually reinforcing, yet economic, social, and cultural rights continue to be marginalized at a time when global inequalities and unilateral coercive measures severely impair human dignity. We draw particular attention to the Special Rapporteur on Unilateral Coercive Measures report on Cuba, which documents the devastating impact of prolonged unilateral sanctions, financial blockades, and overcompliance. These coercive measures cripple economic development, disrupt access to essential health supplies, and directly violate the Charter of the United Nations. Unilateral economic coercion must unconditionally be lifted. Genuine progress requires constructive engagement and technical cooperation, rather than politicization and double standards. My delegation reiterates its commitment to core human rights treaties and calls on this Council to uphold the principles of universality, objectivity, and non-selectivity.

I thank you, Mr. President.
Thank you very much. I give the floor to the distinguished representative of South Sudan.

Mr. Vice President, South Sudan aligns itself with the African Group and NAM statements. We emphasize that the promotion and protection of human rights must be comprehensive, balanced and non-selective, encompassing civil, political, economic, social and cultural rights, including the right to development, in consistency with the Vienna Declaration and the Declaration on the Right to Development. All human rights are universal, indivisible, inalienable interdependent, interrelated and mutually reinforcing. Therefore, the right to development requires more than declarations. It requires practical international cooperation as a universal and inalienable human right. South Sudan believes that human rights, peace and development must advance together. All human rights cannot be fully enjoyed where people lack peace and stability, as well as access to education, health care, food, housing, employment and development, among others. We call upon the international community and our partners to uphold the equal importance and indisability of all human rights, strengthen development, financing, technology transfer, capacity building, and translate international human rights commitments into practical support for countries facing human rights and development challenges. Thank you, Mr. Vice President.
Thank you very much. I give the floor to the distinguished representative of the State of Palestine.

Mr. Vice President, our full statement available on the extranet addresses the Secretary-General's reports on genocide prevention and on the death penalty. The UN Commission of Inquiry and UN Special Rapporteurs have determined that genocide has been committed in Gaza, a finding shared by Human Rights Watch, Amnesty International, and Israeli and Palestinian civil society organizations alike. The Secretary-General's report states that preventing genocide, I quote, "requires political commitment to act early and decisively when warning signs are present," unquote. By his own words, waiting is not an option. Yet the Office of the Special Advisor on the Prevention of Genocide has stated that, I quote, "neither the Secretary-General nor the Special Advisor take a position in relation to ongoing judicial proceedings before the Court," unquote. An ICJ ruling, however, could take years, and nothing in the charter, the court's statute, or its rules require waiting for one. The duty to prevent genocide is a duty of anticipation, not retrospection, a lesson learned at devastating cost from Interahamwe, Rwanda, and Srebrenica. Nor is this standard applied consistently. UN officials have spoken plainly on other international crimes while related cases sat before the ICJ or the ICC. We recognize the weight of this determination. It is precisely because of that weight and the lives at stake that we urge the Secretary General and the Special Adviser to exercise the leadership needed at this moment. I thank you.
Thank you very much. I give the floor to the distinguished representative of Ukraine.

Mr. President, starting from today, the Russian Federation intends to conduct so-called elections. to its State Duma, including in the temporarily occupied territories of Ukraine. Let us be clear, there can be no genuine exercise of political and electoral rights under foreign occupation, coercion, and repression. By imposing its electoral procedures on Ukrainian territory, Russia once again seeks to manufacture an appearance of legitimacy for its illegal occupation and attempted annexation. No ballot, no fabricated turnout, and no staged international observation can change a fundamental fact. These territories are and remain an integral part of Ukraine. The organization of any purported Russian elections there constitutes yet another violation of Ukraine's sovereignty, independence, and territorial integrity, and has no validity under international law. We are particularly concerned by attempts to legitimize this illegal exercise through foreign nationals acting as so-called international observers and through newly created structures designed to imitate credible election monitoring. Ukraine calls upon the international community to unequivocally condemn the organization of these so-called elections. in the temporarily occupied territories of Ukraine and not to recognize their conduct, results, or consequences. Illegal occupation cannot be legitimized through any legal vote. Thank you.
Thank you very much. I give the floor to the distinguished representative of Bahrain.

Thank you, President. We align ourselves with the statement delivered on behalf of the GCC. It's important that we continue to pursue efforts to promote and protect all human rights and to do so in a balanced manner. This includes civil and political rights and economic, social and cultural rights, including the right to development. Bahrain is developing its legislative and institutional arsenal in order to be able to properly promote and protect human rights. and to ensure the full rule of law and justice. We support national institutions, including the national human rights institution. We also raise awareness among society at large about their human rights. We respect and uphold and implement the recommendations from the UPR. The UPR, in our view, is an important tool for supporting and underpinning national efforts in the promotion of human rights and for developing good human rights practices. Bahrain is determined to continue cooperating with this Human Rights Council and its mechanisms because we are of the view that dialogue is essential. Dialogue is also essential for sharing all experiences absent any bias or selectivity. This will assist States in upholding their engagements and commitments and ensure genuine progress in the field of human rights. Thank you very much.
Thank you very much. I give the floor to the distinguished representative of Pakistan.

Thank you, Mr. Vice President. The universality, indivisibility, interdependence and interrelatedness of all human rights constitute a cornerstone in the human rights architecture. We strongly believe that the enjoyment of human rights cannot be separated from the conditions necessary for human dignity and freedom. This is starkly evident in the situations of foreign occupation in Palestine and Indian illegally occupied Jammu and Kashmir. The continued denial of the people's fundamental right to self-determination has impeded the enjoyment of all other human rights. We urge the Council to remain attentive to the human rights of the people in Palestine and Indian illegally occupied Jammu and Kashmir. We also believe that the right to development is indispensable to the full realization of all human rights. Its effective timely implementation must remain a shared global responsibility. Humanity today is confronted by acute challenges, including disregard for international law, climate change, widening inequalities, food insecurity, weaponization of water, xenophobia, religious hatred, and terrorism. To address these challenges, we require enhanced international cooperation and solidarity. Long-standing disputes must be resolved through dialogue, diplomacy, and negotiations in accordance with the UN Charter, international law, and agreements. Pakistan will continue to contribute to the promotion of regional and global peace and stability through dialogue, diplomacy, and its mediation efforts. I thank you, Mr. Vice President.

Thank you very much. That was the last speaker on my list. We shall now turn to the list of speakers from national human rights institutions and non-governmental organizations. And I begin by giving the floor to the Human Rights Commission of the Philippines.

Excellencies, As-Salaam-Alaikum. The people of Myanmar have consistently shown admirable strength, courage, and resilience. I cannot emphasize enough the vital role that women from Myanmar and women human rights defenders in the region play in this fight for the restoration of democracy and resistance against tyranny and hegemony. as they choose to unflinchingly be at the frontlines as mediators, human rights advocates and peacebuilders, despite facing unprecedented security challenges due to the alarming use of conflict-related sexual and gender violence as a military tactic. The Commission on Human Rights of the Philippines, as gender ombud and the national human rights institution of the country, has been actively engaging with the Philippine government, civil society partners, fellow NHRI's, and the diplomatic community to strengthen the regional accountability mechanisms to guarantee the protection of the rights not only of our sisters from Myanmar, but also the rights of fellow Filipino migrant workers caught in the trafficking hubs. I urge all of you to help us continue raising awareness about the human rights and humanitarian crisis in Myanmar. By bringing these issues to the fore, we can contribute to continuing the conversation that triggers political reforms and reconstruction processes and puts women's voices at the center of security, justice, accountability, as well as medical and humanitarian relief.

Thank you very much.
Thank you very much. I give the floor to the European Center for Law and Justice for a video message.

Thank you, Mr. President. I want to commend China on its recent recognition of human rights with the release of Pastor Ezra Jin from prison. But I would like to bring to China's attention that it has another opportunity to champion the human rights of another pastor, Pastor John Saw. Pastor Saw was convicted of a border crossing violation in 2017 while he was providing humanitarian aid to impoverished children. Although Pastor Saw served his entire seven-year sentence, when he was released from prison in March of 2024, he was still unable to return home to the United States due to an administrative law that allows China withhold issuing him a passport for up to three years after his release. But this prohibition is merely discretionary, and a passport could have been issued as early as six months after his release. It has now been two and a half years since Pastor Saw's release from prison, and China is still withholding his passport. Pastor Saw has recently been diagnosed with stage four cancer and desperately needs to return home to his family and receive advanced oncology care in the United States. Issuing Pastor Saw's passport would not be a legal or political concession. It would be a humanitarian act consistent with China's own laws. Therefore, we call on this council to advocate clearly, consistently, and urgently for Pastor Saw's immediate release before it's too late. Thank you.
Thank you. I give the floor to International Pro Bono Legal Services Association Limited.

Excellencies, In July, delegates visited the Lao PDR to observe developments in its legal services system. We were informed that Laos now has nearly 700 practising lawyers nationwide. While that figure may appear modest in absolute terms, the trajectory is clear. In 2016, it had only 188 registered lawyers, and the present figure represents an almost fourfold increase in a decade. Further progress is reflected in the Bar Association's Vision and Strategy Plan, launched in December 2024. It identifies three priorities: strengthening infrastructure, building professional capacity, and advancing gender equality. IPSA recognizes the valuable support of the UNDP in this endeavor. The right to development must benefit everyone, including women, historically marginalized groups, Lao's Ministry of Justice and Bar Association affirmed the commitment to nurturing young and female legal professionals, supporting women lawyers in leadership roles, and promoting awareness in women's rights, commitments we saw translated into action. The Bar Association, furthermore, expressed keen interest in collaboration with legal institutions and civil society organizations in Hong Kong. Such cooperation can advance legal infrastructure, strengthen the rule of law, and build institutional capacity, enhancing rights-based governments through comprehensive accountability mechanisms. While challenges remain, Laos' direction is steady and encouraging. It merits sustained international attention, cooperation, and support. Thank you.
Thank you very much. I give the floor to Al Ain Social Care Foundation for a video statement.

January 2026 marked 20 years of service to these vulnerable groups, with our operations now spanning across Ghana and Afghanistan in addition to Iraq. model of care is rooted in research, expertise, and compassion. Today, we would like to share some stories of the orphan children we have been able to assist. Take Abdullan Sajad in Iraq, for example. Just one month before his passing, their father enrolled them in wrestling at the age of nine, carrying a dream that they would follow in his footsteps. After their father's death, the boys faced financial difficulty, but Al Ain supported them so that they could continue training. Eventually, they went on to win five local titles and a silver medal at the West Asia Championship. In Ghana, little Zainab lost her father when she was 15 months. Al Ain stepped in to assist her and her siblings, providing them with nutritious meals, access to education and clothing. With Al Ain's help, the children have been able to continue with their education, nurturing their passions and allowing them to dream of a better future. In total, we currently support more than 118,000 orphaned youth. Our aim is to ensure that the human rights of orphaned children and widowed mothers are protected and that these groups not only have their basic needs met, but are also permitted to live lives full of hope and happiness. We look forward to another 20 years of service.
Thank you very much. I give the floor to the China NGO Network for International Exchanges.

Mr. President, I'm from the China NGO Network. for international exchanges. We have long been committed to the protection of economic, social, and cultural rights. We firmly believe that civil society is an important force in advancing the development of human rights. Recently, CNI held the Asia Pacific Civil Society Conference in Shandong, China. Civil society representatives widely recognized that the realization of human rights can be separated from equitable and inclusive development, which serves as a solid foundation for the implementation of economic, social, and cultural rights. Together with our Asia-Pacific civil society partners, we put forward 55 partnership initiatives to promote human rights protection and social development. In the future, SENI will continue to work with our member organizations and foreign partners to advance human rights protection and contribute civil society's strength to global human rights development.

We welcome the Office of the High Commissioner's Item 3 report on conscientious objection to military service.

Quakers support all whose conscience calls them to reject military activity. CU Noah has been working for many decades to secure and strengthen the recognition of this right, which is inherent in the right to freedom of thought, conscience and religion, and has been affirmed many times in UN resolutions, all by consensus. Today, the number of armed conflicts is higher than at any time since the UN was founded. We are concerned with the report's finding that the right to conscientious objection to military service is being limited due to armed conflicts. The protection of conscience is most critical when individuals are under the greatest pressure to act against deeply held beliefs. The right to conscientious objection to military service applies at all times. in all circumstances, including during military mobilization and martial law, and for those already serving in armed forces or called up as reservists. Protecting this right is a vital safeguard for democracy and human dignity. We urge all States to implement the report's recommendations, including that conscientious objectors and those supporting them should not be punished, and that those who flee persecution for exercising this right must have access to international protection.
Thank you very much. I give the floor to the Sheikh Taha Alzawi charity organization.

Mr. President, the situation in Libya is characterized by ongoing deprivation of basic services because of power outage, and it is not just a mere instance of deprivation of electricity, but it is a full system of deprivation of rights to water and right to health because the pumping of water has stopped as a result, and infrastructure facilities have been disrupted, as well as the cooling of medication that has been interrupted and no alternatives have been provided, even in the parallel market. This comes with the rise in temperatures to reach 47 degrees, hence the housing facilities have become an environment that is life-threatening. Hence, we recommend a binding protocol that gives an exception to medical facilities and water plants from the overall outage in order to provide a minimum of livability in housing system.

Access to safe and sufficient water is fundamental to the enjoyment of the rights to health, food, sanitation, and adequate standard of living, and a healthy environment.

In Pakistan, the Indus River Basin is central to these rights, supporting communities, agriculture, livelihoods, and ecosystems.

Water scarcity, inefficient use, environmental degradation, climate-related disasters and unequal access disproportionately affect rural

communities, smallholder farmers, women, fishing communities and downstream populations.

We therefore

call for stronger and more transparent water governance, equitable distribution, modernization of irrigation, expanded access to safe

We welcome the OHCHR study on the impact of mental health challenges on the enjoyment of human rights by young people. Mental health is an integral part of their rights, and its challenges can affect young people's ability to fully enjoy and exercise their human rights. Our organizations, IIMA, Vidas International, conducted a global survey that received 1,778 responses across more than 46 countries. The findings highlight barriers that continue to prevent many young people from accessing the support that they need. We therefore urge member states to ensure that mental health services are accessible, affordable, inclusive, and responsive to the needs of young people. Adapt laws, policies and programs that integrate mental health across education, employment and social protection systems consistent with the human rights-based approach. Ensure the meaningful and sustained participation of young people in the design, implementation, monitoring and evaluation of measures that affect their mental health and human rights. commitments must be translated into law, policy, resources, and effective action to ensure that every young person can access the support they need, live with dignity, fully enjoy and exercise their human rights. Thank you.
Thank you very much. I give the floor to Harm Reduction International for a joint statement via a video message.

Excellencies, distinguished delegates, Hum Reduction International and the co-signatories of this statement welcomes three reports before the Council addressing access to medicines and vaccines,

the impact of drug policies on women and girls, and the question of the death penalty. Together, these reports underscore a fundamental

point: drug policy and human rights are inextricably linked, and drug policy debates must fully account for their far-reaching human rights implications.

Criminalization and punitive drug control policies continue to create barriers to health services, disproportionately affect women and other marginalized communities, and drive use of the death penalty worldwide. Yet, while these punitive approaches continue to receive significant public resources, essential health and harm reduction services remain severely underfunded. This is not simply a policy failure. It is also a question of how states choose to use their available resources to fulfill their human rights obligations. We therefore call on states and other relevant actors to divest from punitive drug control and invest in health, community and justice, including voluntary, evidence-based and gender-responsive harm reduction and treatment services. We further call for meaningful participation of women, girls and people who use drugs in shaping drug policies that affect their lives and urge all actors to ensure that drug policies and resources uphold the right to health and human dignity. We call on states, UN agencies and other international actors to ensure that their policies, programs and funding do not contribute to or enable human rights violations in the name of drug control, including definitely for drug-related offenses. We finally call on the Council to adopt a new resolution on drug policy in line with commitment made in 2025.

Thank you.
Thank you very much. I give the floor to United Nations Association of China.

I'm Dr. Kevin Lau, a radiologist from Hong Kong. I read scans. The first vital sign of human rights is whether ordinary lives improve. I read human rights the way I read a scan, life first. Thank you very much. I give the floor to the Youth Parliament for SDGs for a video statement.

President, the realization of rights to development increasingly depends on equitable access to digital technologies and essential public services. India's experience demonstrates how digital public infrastructure can support financial inclusion, access to public services, healthcare, employment, and broader participation in development. Through digital identity, mobile connectivity, interoperable payments, and public service delivery, India has developed a population-scale model offering valuable lessons for the Global South. At the same time, digital transformation must remain firmly grounded in human rights, including privacy, non-discrimination, accessibility, cybersecurity, and accountability. We therefore encourage the Human Rights Council and member states to promote secure and inclusive digital public infrastructure, strengthen South-South and triangular cooperation, and support developing countries through technical assistance, capacity building, and sustainable financing. Digital transformation must serve people and communities, and ensure that technological progress reduces rather than creates inequality. Thank you.
Thank you very much. I give the floor to the IDPC consortium for a video message.

President, I'm making this statement on behalf of IDPC, Cooperacion Mujeres Libres Colombia, the International Network of Formerly Incarcerated Women, which brings together hundreds of women in more than 30 countries on six continents. I also deliver this statement on behalf of five further organizations. Punitive drug policies are a leading cause of women's incarceration, with devastating and disproportionate impacts on the women themselves, but also their families and communities. Women's pathways into drug use or the drug trade are often linked to gender and structural inequalities, including poverty and gender-based violence. Deprivation of liberty further exacerbates these conditions and inequalities. Those of us who have lived experience of this must be centred in shaping and implementing policy alternatives. We advocate for approaches rooted in care, not punishment, and for channeling resources to programs that address the inequalities and trauma faced by women who are criminalized, that keep families together, and that lead to gender and socioeconomic justice. We therefore welcome the OHCHR report on the impacts of drug policies on women. and call on the Human Rights Council to continue to address the human rights implications of drug policy, including by the adoption of a new resolution on drug policy. Thank you very much.
Thank you. I give the floor to the Association d'Entraide Medicale Guinee for a video statement.

Mr. President, after more than three years of war, civilians in the Sudan continue to pay a heavy price amid ongoing violations, displacement, the destruction of homes, health facilities and infrastructure, and the severe deterioration of access to food, water, healthcare and education. Recent international reports continue to document serious violations, including violations attributed to the Sudanese armed forces and authorities associated with them, as well as the devastating impact of war on the civil, political, economic, and social rights of the Sudanese people. We welcome recent international and regional efforts to receive the political process and reaffirm, as the Quintet recently stressed, that there is no military solution to the conflict. We call upon the Sudanese authorities to engage seriously in a negotiated peace process leading to a cessation of hostilities, the protection of civilians, and a path towards democratic civilian rule. We also call for international pressure on external actors whose support to the Sudanese armed forces contributes to the continuation of the war and violations, and for an end to such support. Protecting the rights of the Sudanese people requires ending the war, ensuring accountability for violations, and paving the way for sustainable peace and civilian governance that respects human rights. Thank you.
Thank you very much. I give the floor to the Beijing Guangming Charity Foundation for a video statement.

Mr. President, I'm the President of Beijing Guangming Charity Foundation. For 12 years, our foundation has run the STAR project for autistic people, focusing on digital inclusion for neurodivergent people. Deaf and hard of hearing people face digital barriers as digital products are not designed to be accessible, support services lack standards, cross-border services interrupt poorly. These shortcomings hamper their equal participation in education, employment, social life, contrary to the inclusive spirit of the CRPD and the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development. Last July, at the side event of HL Political Forum, we published three group standards on sustainable development. They show that standardization offers an effective solution to inclusion. To tackle digital exclusion, we need a unified, practical, and internationally interoperable system of standards. Standardization can bridge the digital divide as it sets rules for accessible design, unified rehabilitation procedures, create common evaluation mechanisms that would make services replicable and practical experience shareable. We propose using UN mechanisms to advance international standards by sharing Chinese practices at no cost so as to safeguard vulnerable groups' equal human rights. The video stopped.
Thank you very much. I give the floor to the Blue Tree Foundation for a video message.

Thank you, Mr. President. The Blue Tree Foundation, BTF, a youth NGO from the Republic of Korea dedicated to building a society free from violence, draws the Council's attention to profit-driven vigilantism disguised as protecting the freedom of expression and the right to record. Lawful recording promotes accountability and protects individuals. However, auditors, who are content creators who claim to defend public rights, deliberately provoke confrontations, disrupt public spaces, and sometimes disclose personal information for views and revenue. Their videos mobilize audiences to threaten, condemn, and target individuals, which causes secondary harm. This form of abuse also greatly affects youth, who are particularly vulnerable to online exposure and harassment. In the Republic of Korea, a teenager accused of wrongdoing was filmed being coerced into kneeling and apologizing. The teenager's personal information was circulated online, attracting widespread hate and reaching 7 million views and 230,000 shares. This is not accountability.

It is harassment disguised as justice.

We urge member states of the Council to first distinguish public interest recording from targeted recording harassment,

and second, ensure accountability for deliberate provocation and exposure of personal information for profit. Freedom of expression must protect the vulnerable and must never, under any circumstances, turn them into targets for profit. Thank you.
Thank you very much. I give the floor to the Luis de la Calle Foundation.

The next cycle includes Iraq and Kenya with a global arts event on 18th March 2017, marking the 10th anniversary of the Beirrut Declaration on Faith for Rights. Mr. Vice President, through art, children live human rights and make their voices heard globally. Let their voices and creativity shape the world now. Thank you, Mr. Vice President.
Thank you very much. I give the floor for a joint statement to Americans for Democracy and Human Rights in Bahrain.

Mr. President, we draw the Council's attention to the arbitrary detention of minors in Bahrain, including amid the ongoing regional conflict. On the 8th of March 2026, 16-year-old Mahdi Al-Mu'adhdan was arrested without a warrant, allegedly for filming a fire near his school. Denied all outside contact for a month, he was deprived of education, family visits, and legal counsel, while being subjected to threats, physical beatings, and sectarian abuse. On the 21st of July, he was sentenced to six years for terrorism and arson. The situation of minors in the Dry Rock Prison has sharply deteriorated. On the 25th of August 2026, riot forces stormed building 17 to disperse a peaceful sit-in protesting religious insult and poor conditions, causing injuries, suffocation, and a communications blackout. Ten minors remain in solitary confinement, facing ongoing psychological and physical abuse. Hence, we urge the Council to put an end to the suffering of those detainees and to call on Bahrain to put an end to the arbitrary detention and solitary confinement of children and carry out independent investigations in these abuses and hold those responsible accountable. Thank you.
Thank you very much. I give the floor to Agence Internationale pour le Developpement.

Mr. Vice President, the International Agency for Development wishes to draw the Council's attention to the need to address migration through an approach grounded in human dignity, the protection of individuals, and shared responsibility among countries of origin, transit, and destination. In this regard, Morocco has developed a significant experience in North Africa, notably through its national immigration and asylum strategy, migrants organization operation, and policies aimed at ensuring their access to essential services, and their social and economic integration. Its position as a country of origin, transit, and now how also of destination also confront the kingdom with complex challenges, particularly in border management and the fight against human traffic and migrant smuggling networks. Our organization stress that the protection of fundamental rights must remain at the heart of any immigration policy, including during border control operation, and therefore encourages Morocco to continue its efforts to strengthen protection and redress mechanisms, and to increase cooperation with African and European countries. Migration is a collective responsibility. Transit states must not become solely responsible for the consequences of crises, inequalities, and migratory movements whose causes extend far beyond their borders. Thank you.
Thank you very much. I give the floor to Beijing NGO Association for International Exchanges for a video message.

Beijing NGO Association for International Exchanges is committed to helping local NGOs engage in global governance.

Protecting the right to development is key focus of our work. And we believe that concrete action is essential. Thank you, Chair. We express our deep concern over the increasing arrests of political opponents in the Islamic Republic of Iran and draw the attention of the Working Group on Arbitrary Detention to this alarming trend. We also strongly condemn the issuance and implementation of death sentences against detainees and political opponents. These punishments have become a tool for suppressing opponents, spreading fear and terror throughout society, and punishing individuals who exercise their fundamental rights. Since the beginning of 2026, more than 1,000 people have been executed in Iran.
